questions.q: What problem does a periodic snapshot fact table solve that a transaction fact table doesn't?
options: It provides a value for every entity at every fixed time interval, even when nothing happened to that entity that day
It stores more decimal places of precision than a transaction fact table
It removes the need for any dimension keys
It automatically deletes old rows to save space
questions.explain: A transaction table only has a row when an event occurs; a periodic snapshot loads a row for every entity on a schedule regardless of whether anything changed, which is exactly what a question like "stock level at the end of each day" needs.

questions.q: In the f_InventorySnapshot example, what is the correct one-sentence grain statement?
options: One row per product per warehouse per snapshot date
One row per product, ever
One row per warehouse per year
One row per stock movement transaction
questions.explain: The table loads a row for every product-warehouse combination on every snapshot date, whether or not the quantity on hand changed.

questions.q: Why is it valid to sum QuantityOnHand across products on a single snapshot date, but not valid to sum it across multiple snapshot dates?
options: Summing across products on one day gives a real total; summing across dates double-counts the same stock that was simply still there, which is what makes the measure semi-additive
SQL Server physically prevents summing a column across more than one date
QuantityOnHand should never be summed under any circumstance
Because the column is stored as DECIMAL instead of INT
questions.explain: This is the defining behavior of a semi-additive measure: valid across some dimensions (products, warehouses), invalid across the time dimension.

questions.q: Why did Microsoft's guidance choose a daily snapshot for inventory instead of a transaction fact table recording every stock movement?
options: There could be millions of movements a day, and if the analysis only needs end-of-day trends, storing every movement is expensive and unnecessary
SQL Server cannot store more than one row per product
Transaction fact tables are not allowed to reference a Product dimension
Periodic snapshots always use less disk space than any transaction table, regardless of the use case
questions.explain: This is a deliberate performance and grain choice: the snapshot gives you the answer the analysis actually needs at a fraction of the row count.

questions.q: If you need to see a trend in a loyalty-points balance over several months, what should you do instead of summing the balance across those months?
options: Take the average or last value of the balance across the period
Sum the balance across months, since it's a numeric column
Multiply the balance by the number of months
Convert the measure into a dimension attribute first
questions.explain: Because a periodic snapshot measure is semi-additive across time, a trend needs an average or a point-in-time value, never a straight SUM() across snapshot dates.
